paras: The attempted lynching of a Chinese boy on Roberts Island took place on August 23, 1881, when an 11-year-old Chinese boy accused of setting fire to a grain stack on a ranch near Stockton, California, was captured and tied by his cue to a header-wagon. According to the only dispatch on the case, he would have been hanged had women on the ranch not interfered, and he was instead arraigned in court at Stockton. The Sacramento Daily Record-Union reported it as a "Narrow Escape of a Chinese Incendiary from Lynching," and a Nevada paper reprinted the item.

The fire was set on the ranch of R. H. McCoy on Roberts Island on the Tuesday before the dispatch. A workman said he saw the boy place a piece of paper in the stack and strike a match, which went out, and then a second, after which the flames ran up the side of the stack. The boy ran for the tules and hid there, while the fire was put out "after much difficulty."

He was then captured and tied to the rack of a header-wagon by his cue. The dispatch does not say who caught him or how many were involved, stating only that "had it not been for the interference of the women on the place he would have been strung up."

The boy was arraigned in court at Stockton the following day on the charge of setting the fire, and his examination was set for Saturday. No report of the examination or its result appears in the coverage, and no one is reported to have been charged over the attempt to hang him.

The story reached print as a Stockton dispatch dated August 25 in the "Pacific Coast" column of the Sacramento Daily Record-Union on August 26. Its headline called the boy a "Chinese Incendiary," treating the arson charge as settled, and presented the near-hanging as a narrow escape without comment on his captors. The Silver State of Unionville, Nevada, reprinted the text almost word for word among its "Telegraphic Items" on August 27, dropping the headline and the examination date and giving the owner as "H. R. McCoy." No Black newspaper coverage from 1881 is available for comparison.

The two printings differ on the arraignment date: the Record-Union's dispatch, dated August 25, says "yesterday," while the Silver State reprint says "Last Thursday," and the dated original is the better evidence.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of a Chinese boy on Roberts Island
bases: A Chinese boy accused of arson was captured and tied by his cue to a header-wagon, and the dispatch says he would have been 'strung up' but for the women on the ranch, under the headline 'Narrow Escape ... from Lynching' (A2); the target was Chinese, not Black.

No one was killed: the boy was arraigned in court the next day (A2). The captors acted without lawful authority over an arson accusation, but their number is not given; this was at most an attempted lynching, and its target was Chinese (A2, A3).
The only account is one Stockton dispatch (A2); the Silver State item is a reprint of the same text (A3), not an independent report.

accounts.label: Stockton dispatch
accounts.gist: The boy was seen firing the stack, fled to the tules, was captured and tied to a header-wagon by his cue, and would have been strung up but for the women on the place; he was arraigned and his examination set for Saturday.

framing.detail: The Record-Union ran it under 'Narrow Escape of a Chinese Incendiary from Lynching', treating the arson as established and the near-hanging as a narrow escape, without comment on the captors.
The Silver State reprinted the dispatch almost word for word among its 'Telegraphic Items', without a headline.

conflicts.note: The Record-Union carries the dated Stockton dispatch; the Silver State reworded the opening when reprinting it, so the Aug. 24 date is the better evidence.
